name: Dag Nasty
label: Dischord
lede: Four singers, one guitarist who never left, and a 1986 record that taught hardcore how to carry a tune without losing its nerve.

eras.title: Minor Threat's guitarist wants a melody
eras.text: Minor Threat was done and Brian Baker had songs that were faster than pop and catchier than anything hardcore was allowing itself. He pulled a rhythm section out of Bloody Mannequin Orchestra and a singer out of the DC scene, and by Halloween they had a whole album on tape.

years.h: Baker builds a band out of Bloody Mannequin Orchestra
years.p: Drummer [[Colin Sears|c9bbc03c-06bf-4c37-9f54-e95b51aede4c]] and bassist [[Roger Marbury|c24bb563-e743-4478-9380-fe877ca4031f]] come over from Bloody Mannequin Orchestra. [[Shawn Brown|e39556a4-0d8f-4138-bc18-a54d3a66eefe]] sings. Baker is the one with the plan.

years.cap: The first Dag Nasty: Brown, Baker, Marbury, Sears
years.h: Halloween at Inner Ear: a whole album, then the shelf
years.p: With [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] producing in Don Zientara's Arlington basement, the band cuts nine songs on Halloween Day. Then Brown is out, and the tape goes in a drawer for twenty-five years.
years.xp:
Dischord's own notes say it plainly: the album was shelved after Shawn Brown departed, and in early 1986 the band recut the whole thing with a new singer. The songs survived. The performance didn't, not until 2010.

Brown went on to front [[Swiz|eea2f3d8-1e94-436c-ae66-4633f99f55be]], one of the harder-edged DC bands of the next few years, and came back to Dag Nasty on his own terms more than two decades later.

eras.title: Three singers in one year
eras.text: The record that made Dag Nasty's name happened in a hurry, with a Boston singer who wasn't going to stay. By the end of the year the band had lost him, toured half the country with a replacement found through a classified ad, and quit.

years.h: A Boston hardcore singer comes south
years.p: [[Dave Smalley|c637a12d-5f55-4b83-bef0-a56b3c1e326c]] of [[DYS|f012c04d-96ca-47dd-9359-3bb11fed88b5]] takes the mic. A Boston straight-edge shouter now fronting the most tuneful band in DC.
A club show that ends up on tape. Four live tracks from that night later ride along as bonus cuts on the Can I Say CD.

Recut at Inner Ear with MacKaye producing. Baker plays a '70s Les Paul goldtop through a Marshall, and an MXR chorus pedal he found lying around the studio ends up all over the record. Hardcore with choruses you could sing back.
years.xp:
Eight of the songs had been around since the Brown session and were, in Baker's words to Guitar World, slightly tarted up for the new take. The borrowed chorus pedal is the secret ingredient: it gives the guitars that wide, ringing sheen that set the record apart from the DC hardcore around it.

The album's reach runs long. Its songs are cited in histories of emo, Circles turned up on a Tony Hawk game soundtrack, and Blink-182's Travis Barker has the title tattooed on his chest.

q: Our singer decides he's going to go do graduate school.
years.h: The big tour, and the singer goes to school
years.p: Dag Nasty land the opening slot on a big summer run with the [[Descendents|f035837e-4117-438d-a524-cacf43500e68]]. Smalley leaves for graduate school before it starts.
years.xp:
It was the break a young band waits for, and it came apart on the calendar. Smalley chose school, and Baker was left with dates on the books and nobody to sing them.

The fix came from the classifieds, and the new voice changed the band's direction for the next two years.

years.cap: Peter Cortner, recruited from the classifieds
years.h: A singer from the want ads
years.p: The band places an ad in a local paper and finds [[Peter Cortner|66e99d7d-3c1e-429b-a95c-5591f9278616]]. He learns the set and heads out with the Descendents across half the United States.
Home from the tour and a few local shows, the band calls it. Baker heads to Los Angeles and starts Doggy Style with Descendents bassist [[Doug Carrion|bdc25394-8356-4bcd-9118-520f17af9333]].

eras.title: Wig out, then Field Day
eras.text: Baker and Carrion came back east and put Dag Nasty back together around Cortner's voice, which pushed the band further toward pop. Two records in a year, a move off Dischord to Giant, and then the original run was over.

years.h: Back from LA with a new bass player
years.p: Baker, Cortner, Sears and Carrion restart the band. Marbury declines to rejoin.
Recorded at Inner Ear in March with MacKaye and Zientara. Cortner's first album and the band's second: brighter, poppier, still fast. Alternative Press later put it in the emo canon.
A single for Giant Records, and a sign of where the band was headed next.

years.h: Sears out, Scott Garrett in for the Giant sessions
years.p: The founding drummer is gone by the time the band cuts its third album. Scott Garrett plays on it.

The ambitious one: pop hooks, hardcore speed, metal muscle, a cover of [[The Ruts|a2f938aa-1aa3-474b-a070-762067274eab]] and a remake of Under Your Influence. Robert Christgau gave it an A minus. Wikipedia credits it with 30,000-plus copies in its first year.
After the Field Day tour, Dag Nasty break up. In 2009 Baker was still calling Cortner a really good lyricist and talking about another record with him.

eras.title: Dale Nixon plays guitar
eras.text: Baker went off to play hard rock and signed a contract that followed him back to punk. The Can I Say line-up got one more album out of it anyway, with the guitarist hiding behind a borrowed name, and then Baker took the job that defined the rest of his career.

years.p: With Chris Gates, formerly of Austin's Big Boys, he starts the Los Angeles hard rock band Junkyard. A long way from Inner Ear.
Selfless Records puts out a set of pre-Can I Say recordings.

Smalley, Marbury and Sears back together, cut in Los Angeles in the summer of 1991 with [[Brett Gurewitz|cd40188b-ea30-4729-bebb-e8c5091c9d02]] producing. The guitarist is credited as Dale Nixon: Baker was under contract to Junkyard.
years.xp:
Dale Nixon is a punk in-joke with a history: it's the alias Greg Ginn used for his bass parts on [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]]'s My War. Baker borrowing it for a contractual workaround is about as DC-to-LA as a credit line gets.

The Washington Post called the album first-rate. It was the Can I Say band, minus the name on the sleeve.

years.p: Baker turns down a touring spot with R.E.M. and takes Gurewitz's place in Bad Religion. He's still there three decades on.

eras.title: Back to the basement
eras.text: Dag Nasty came home to Inner Ear for a full-length that sounded like hardcore again, then Dischord opened the vault on the session that started everything.

years.p: Recorded at Inner Ear in January with Don Zientara and former Minor Threat bassist [[Steve Hansgen|cd469927-13a8-4d0b-8898-01c6856f5878]] producing. Smalley sings again, the tempos go back up. Reviews were split: Drowned in Sound liked it, Pitchfork didn't.
The Halloween 1985 session, restored from the master tapes, finally out. The Can I Say songs as they first sounded, with the singer who was there first.

eras.title: The first singer gets his turn
eras.text: The line-up that had been a footnote became the working band. A documentary about the DC scene brought them to the stage, and a new session at Inner Ear gave Shawn Brown his first Dag Nasty release that didn't come out of the archive.

years.h: The original four announce a show
years.p: Brown, Baker, Marbury and Sears, together on stage for the first time since 1985.
The original line-up plays DC's Black Cat in support of Salad Days: The DC Punk Revolution. [[Government Issue|9b952ee8-d45d-4a26-8066-57849d871e06]] are on the bill too.
The original four record two songs with MacKaye and Zientara in the same basement where the Halloween tape was made.
Two songs, Cold Heart and Wanting Nothing. The first new music with Brown singing, released three decades after he was replaced.
A European run, Punk Rock Bowling in Las Vegas, and a June 11 date in Asbury Park, New Jersey.

sources.title: Guitar World: The rise and fall of Dag Nasty
